title: Visakha's eight gifts
hook: a downpour, a mistaken servant, and eight gifts nobody else had thought of.
carry: visakha's giving: notice who got missed
tomorrow: if nobody is giving you orders, why keep a rule at all?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a prince gave past every limit, and the tradition argued with him about it. Generosity costs. Today's giving costs much less money, and much more attention.

On moving day, most friends bring boxes. One friend notices that nobody has eaten since breakfast. So what can you give in a single day that costs no money at all? Drop into a downpour in the city of Savatthi. A servant girl runs back through the rain to her mistress, Visakha, with strange news. She was sent to tell the monks their meal is ready, she says, but there are no monks at the monastery. Only naked ascetics, standing out in the rain.
screen: `BOXES, OR LUNCH?` → `A DOWNPOUR IN SAVATTHI.` → `"THERE ARE NO MONKS THERE."`

segments.voice: Visakha understands at once. The monks are bathing in the rain, and they have nothing to bathe in. She sends the girl back. After the meal, as the monastic rule books tell it, she asks the Buddha for eight boons, gifts she'll give for as long as she lives. Cloths for the monks to bathe in when it rains. Food for monks arriving in town, tired, who don't know the streets yet. Food for monks leaving, so they don't miss their caravan while begging. Food for the sick. Food for whoever is nursing the sick, so they don't go hungry while caring. Medicine. A steady supply of rice gruel. And bathing cloths for the nuns. The Buddha asks her why, and she has a reason for every one. Listen to that list again. The food cost money. The noticing didn't. She saw the newcomer, the traveler, the patient, and the person everyone forgets: the one doing the caring. That's the gift under all her gifts. And it's what a day of giving can be. Time. Attention. Food, if you have it. Praise, honestly meant. Visakha's eight boons start with her eyes.
screen: `MONKS IN THE RAIN.` · `EIGHT BOONS, FOR LIFE.` · `FEED THE ONE WHO NURSES.` · `THE NOTICING COST NOTHING.` · then, large: `A DAY OF GIVING.`

segments.voice: Say softly, out loud, the name of one person you'll see today. Then name one thing they might need that nobody has noticed: a little time, real attention, a meal, an honest word of praise. Sit with that person in mind, the way Visakha sat with the monks in the rain.
A day of giving: time, attention, food and praise, given where you've noticed the need. Visakha's eight boons began that way.
Hold onto this: Visakha's giving, which starts with noticing who got missed. Talk tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1548 COUNTS.` → `THE TEN PERFECTIONS · DAY 3 OF 30.` → `TOMORROW: IF NOBODY GIVES ORDERS, WHY KEEP A RULE?`

howItsDone: Lay Buddhists give food, robes and medicine to monastics, and temples hold days of giving; teachers also name time, attention and kind speech as gifts anyone can give.

chat.says: garage sale chaos. ava's little brother is crying about selling his bike. i have $0 left. what do i do?
options: Give what's free: time and attention. Sit with him and notice what he actually needs.
Nothing, honestly. With no money left there isn't much you can give at a sale.
Promise to buy the bike back for him later. A real gift is something you pay for.

Visakha.meaning: a laywoman of the Buddha's time, known for her giving

Savatthi.meaning: a city where the Buddha stayed and taught

ascetics.meaning: wandering holy people who gave up comforts, some unclothed

boons.meaning: favors asked and granted; here, gifts Visakha asked to give

sources.ref: Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga 8.15 (Visakha's eight boons: rain-bathing cloths for the Sangha, food for incoming monks, food for outgoing monks, food for the sick, food for those who nurse the sick, medicine for the sick, a constant supply of rice gruel, bathing cloths for the nuns; the servant mistakes the monks bathing in the rain for naked ascetics; Visakha gives her reasons)

notes: Vinaya Mahavagga 8.15 paraphrased. Confirm the setting (Savatthi), the order of the eight boons and the reasons given (newcomers don't know the streets; departing monks would miss their caravan; nurses would go hungry).
'Visakha understands at once' compresses the text; confirm. The servant's line is quoted in screen marks as a paraphrase, not a translation.
'Time, attention, food, praise' come from the outline; the Vinaya story supplies the noticing behind them. 'Praise' is not claimed for Visakha.
